abstract.p: From an evolutionary perspective, all organisms have two purposes: self-preservation and reproduction, in which immobility responses (IR) are implicated, these are ancestral survival strategies used to avoid serious injury or death. Immobility responses are adaptive reactions present in many species across virtually the entire phylogenetic spectrum, characterized by behavioral arrest and reduced responsiveness, serving evolutionary roles in prey–predator, mating, and offspring-carrying contexts. Several brain structures—including the brainstem, limbic system, striatum, and cortex—modulate IR by integrating fear, motor, and sensory processes; moreover, distinct drugs such as antipsychotics and morphine can induce IR through monoaminergic and endorphinic pathways. Immobility responses have been referred to by various terms, including animal hypnosis, catalepsy, catatonia, cataplexy, death feigning, and dorsal immobility, among others. The most commonly employed laboratory methods for inducing and replicating immobility responses are described herein. Experimental animal models reported in this work (frog, iguana, duck, rabbit, and rat) reproduce IR under controlled conditions, providing valuable insights into motor inhibition, defensive behaviors, and catatonic states.

sec.title: Background
sec.p:
From an evolutionary biology perspective, every living being fulfills two fundamental purposes. One of them is reproduction, needed to ensure the preservation of the species. The other purpose is self-preservation primarily consisting of eating and avoiding being eaten. Both of these are somehow linked to defense and protection mechanisms, including immobility responses. The immobility response (IR) is a state of complete motor inhibition and reduced responsiveness. Both immobility and mobility are neurobiological reflexes, active survival strategies serving distinct adaptive purposes [1,2]. Many animals freeze in response to fear triggered by visual, auditory, or mechanical stimuli, as well as environmental factors such as temperature or food availability, characterized by reduced movement, breathing and sometimes emotional response. Prey–predator models across vertebrates and invertebrates show that IR enhances survival, since an immobile prey often prevents predators from detecting them or causes predators decreased aggression or interest. The duration of IR varies with environmental risk and refuge availability [3]. Prey assesses danger and adjusts behavior, accordingly, remaining transiently aware of their surroundings. The adaptive value of IR is underscored by its phylogenetic conservation—from amphibians like frogs to mammals such as rabbits—and its link to fitness-related behaviors like mating. For example, females adopt a lordosis posture during copulation which can reduce physical damage and protect the individual in extreme situations such as domination and sexual asssault. Neonates display a similar posture when carried by the dam (Fig. 1) [1]. Although mechanisms remain unclear, brainstem and basal forebrain structures are involved. The limbic system enhances IR through fear, the neocortex inhibits it, and dopaminergic blockade in the striatum facilitates IR via the basal ganglia. In rats, IR can be induced by dorsal immobility (lifting the rat by the neck) or by clamping the dorsal surface of the neck while the animal lies supine [[1], [4]]. As these systems mature, IR duration decreases, explaining its brevity in adults[5]. This phenomenon is most evident in neonatal and young animals, reflecting the naturally adopted posture when pups are carried by the dam (Fig. 1). During the first two postnatal days (PND), pups show no limb flexion; from PND 2 to 40, they adopt a ventrally flexed posture similar to that during neck clamping. As maternal carrying diminishes, the response gradually fades and disappears by PND 40 [1].Fig. 1
Dam transporting its pup. The pup exhibits a posture that facilitates carrying. At postnatal day (PND) 0, limb flexion is absent, but as the pups grow and gain weight, it becomes increasingly difficult for the dam to carry them, and consequently they are dragged.Fig 1

IR can also be pharmacologically elicited. In this context, catalepsy and catatonia are distinguished. Catalepsy, typically induced by neuroleptics such as haloperidol [6,7], features widely spread limbs providing broad postural support, with static balance reflexes—air-righting, contact-righting, bracing, and clinging—preserved [8,9]. Catatonia, often following morphine administration, involves limbs held close to the body and suppression of balance reflexes, including bracing reactions. Immobility from neck clamping closely resembles morphine-induced catatonia, as both inhibit these reflexes [6].

This work summarizes experimental procedures used to induce immobility in mammals. Rats are the most studied species, followed by rabbits. The technique applied in rabbits closely parallels those used in frogs and ducks, producing comparable behavioral outcomes.

sec.title: Method details
sec.p: To evaluate IR across species, different methods can be applied and compared. In amphibians such as frogs, IR can be easily elicited just by inverting the animal and restricting its movement. In reptiles, birds and some mammals such as rabbits and neonatal rats, the IR can be induced like the amphibians. Importantly, none of these approaches require specialized equipment or pharmacological intervention.

In these cases, fear appears to be the psychological factor playing an important role, as it is well known that some animals, such as mice, when attacked by predators, may fall prey to fear and remain completely immobile, similar to tonic immobility (TI). The vestibular stimulation caused by quickly inverting the animal is associated with the immobility reflex [10].

sec.title: Immobility response in amphibians
sec.p: The IR is a well-documented survival mechanism in anurans facing imminent predation (e.g.,frogs). The methodology employed to elicit this defense mechanism under experimental conditions is described below.

list-item.p: A flat surface.
A wet cloth

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
To induce the IR in frogs, place the animal in supine position and gently rub the abdomen with slight pressure for approximately 8 s before releasing it slowly (Fig. 2B). Following this procedure, frogs typically remain immobile for a prolonged period. To make the frog return to its prone position, a loud sound must be induced to interrupt the immobility response. To prevent skin damage, keep the body moist throughout the test (Fig. 2C-D).Fig. 2
(A) Frog in prone position. (B) Holding the grog and applying gentle pressure on the abdominal region. (C) Place the frog on its back, rub the abdominal region and slowly release it. (D) The animal remains completely immobile.Fig 2

sec.title: Immobility response in reptiles
sec.p: Tonic immobility has been studied in geckos, it was tested as the ability to distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar handlers, revealing sex-specific differences [11]. In snakes, death feigning was reported in 66 % of wild-caught individuals but was absent in hatchlings from laboratory-incubated eggs [12]. Some wild snakes remained immobile even after release, occasionally adopting a supine position for up to 10 min [13]. In lizards, IR has also been examined following drug administration [14]. The methodology described in the present study was applied to an iguana using the same procedure as in frogs.

list-item.p: A flat surface, usually a table.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
To induce the IR in iguanas, hold the animal by the body and place it in the supine position (Fig. 3B). Gently rub the abdominal region while applying slight pressure, then release the animal slowly (Fig. 3C).Fig. 3
(A) The iguana in a prone position. (B) Rubbing its abdomen to induce immobility. (C) Top view of the iguana resting on its back while it remains in an immobile state, it shows a slight ventroflexion of its body.Fig 3

list-item.p: A flat surface.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
To induce immobility in large birds, restrain the animal by the legs and neck, whereas for small birds, hold the body and invert it (Fig. 4B). Once positioned supine, apply gentle pressure to the chest while lightly stimulating the animal, then release it gradually (Fig. 4B-C). Repeating this procedure in the same subject induces immobility more rapidly and for a longer duration (Fig. 4D).Fig. 4
(A) Duck in prone position. (B) Holding the body of the duck and turned upside down. (C) In supine position, apply gentle pressure to the animal’s chest, while it is softly stimulated and gradually released. (D) The animal remains completely immobile.Fig 4

sec.title: Immobility response in mammals
sec.p: Some mammals also exhibit TI as a defense mechanism, including opossums, rabbits, bovines, among others. In the laboratory, the IR can be easily induced in rabbits.

list-item.p: A flat surface.
Protective gloves to avoid being scratched.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
To induce the IR in rabbits, hold the animal by the forelimbs and hindlimbs (Fig. 5B). Quickly rotate it and place it in the supine position (Fig. 5C). Once supine, rub the abdominal region repeatedly for 10 s. After release, confirm immobility (Fig. 5D).Fig. 5
A) Rabbit in a prone position. B) The rabbit is held by its forelimbs and hindlimbs. C) Place the rabbit with its ventral side facing up and rub the abdominal region. D)The animal remains completely immobile.Fig 5

sec.title: Immobility response in rat
sec.p: The rat is one of the most widely used animals in the study of behavior and physiology in general. Therefore, it is important to understand how certain immobility responses are induced in order to study the pathways involved in these responses, such as the dopaminergic and endorphinergic pathways, which may be therapeutic targets for neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative diseases. As mentioned above, the adult rat no longer exhibits the TI response, but it does exhibit dorsal and clamping immobility responses. These behaviors require persistent stimulus to the neck. Here, we describe some of the most relevant kinds of immobility responses.

list-item.p: Timer: either a chronometer or video recording to register test duration.
Disinfectant: 30 % ethanol applied between trials.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
The animal is gently grasped by the scruff, between the base of the skull and the back of the ears and then lifted so that no part of its body is in contact with any surface. Immobility was timed from the onset of the response to the appearance of escape movements or a maximum of 180 s (Fig. 6).Fig. 6
Dorsal immobility. The skin is grasped of the back of the neck between the base of the skull and the back of the ears.Fig 6

list-item.p: A flat surface, usually a table.
Two clamps
Timer: Registered by chronometer or video camera
Material for clean-up: Usually paper towels to clean urine and feces
Disinfectant: We use ethanol 30 % for general cleaning.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
The IR is induced by applying two clamps between the base of the skull and the back of the ears. The pressure is sufficient to lift the whole animal body by the clamp (Fig. 7). Once the clamps are applied, the rat is turned and held on the table in a supine position until it is still, then it is released (Fig. 7C). Time was measured from when the rat was released until it recovered its prone position, or 180 s[8].Fig. 7
(A) Applying two clamps between the base of the skull and the back of the ears. (B) The rat is turned and held on the table in a supine position until it is still, (C) then it is released.Fig 7

Note. Immobility by clamping is shown at all ages tested, from day 5 to 90. The clamps were wrapped with soft material like masking tape or could be fabric, to avoid harming the rat with the edges of the clamp.

sec.title: Immobility responses induced by: lesions, animal models for neuropsychiatric disorders, and some drugs
sec.p: There are other forms of immobility that occur after the administration of drugs or specific lesions in the brain or in animal models in rat. These responses can be assesed through complementary techniques that involve movements or positions considered uncomfortable for the rat, including clinging, bracing reaction to displacement, contact righting, and air righting.

sec.title: Vertical clinging
sec.p: Clinging is widely employed as an assay for drug-induced catalepsy [15,16]. The test is based on the disinhibition of tonic grasping: once the grasp reflex is elicited, cataleptic rats fail to release their hold for two minutes or longer [17].

list-item.p: Plexiglass frame with two horizontal 2 mm diameter steel bars mounted 8 cm apart.
Timer: a chronometer or video recording to register test duration.
Disinfectant: 30 % ethanol applied between trials.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p:
Tonic grasp was tested by registering the duration of upright clinging to two horizontal steel bars, with 2 mm in diameter and vertically spaced 8 cm apart, mounted on a plexiglass frame. The initial posture adopted when placed in the clinging position was recorded [18] (Fig. 8A). Counting was stopped as soon as the animal made any movement that disrupted the initial position.Fig. 8
(A) Vertical clinging. Upright clinging to two horizontal steel bars 2 mm in diameter and 8 cm vertically apart mounted on a plexiglass frame. (B) Bracing reaction in response to displacement. An externally applied force that attempts to move them forward, backward, or sideways which lead to the maintenance of strong paw contact with the ground.Fig 8

sec.title: Bracing reaction in response to displacement
sec.p: Cataleptic animals actively resist externally applied forces that attempt to move them forward, backward, or sideways. This resistance is mediated by strong positive supporting reactions of the limbs, which maintain firm paw contact with the ground [18].

list-item.p: Flat surface.
Timer: a chronometer or video recording to register test duration.
Disinfectant: 30 % ethanol applied between trials.
Paper towels to remove urine and feces.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p: To assess the bracing reaction, gently displace the animal forward, backward, or sideways while maintaining paw contact with the surface. The response is considered positive when the limbs follow the direction of displacement[19] and negative when the limbs remain static [20] (Fig. 8B).

list-item.p: Flat surface.
Timer: a chronometer or video recording to register test duration.
Disinfectant: 30 % ethanol applied between trials.
Paper towels to remove urine and feces.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p: To assess immobility, turn the rat gently and hold it in the supine position on the table until immobility is established [18]. Record the duration from the time the animal is placed supine until it regains its prone position. In a similar manner, test animals by placing them in the lateral position on the table [21].

list-item.p: Flat surface.
Foam cushion 30 × 20 × 5 cm.
Video camera mounted on a tripod.
Disinfectant: 30 % ethanol.

sec.title: Procedure
sec.p: To evaluate the air-righting reflex, hold the rat in the supine position approximately 40 cm above a foam cushion and release it to allow free fall (four trials per rat). Assess righting ability by whether the animal lands in the prone or supine position. Record the duration from the moment of release until righting occurs. Use this test to evaluate differences in righting reflex behavior [18,21].

sec.p: Not applicable.

sec.title: Ethics statements
sec.p: All animal experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with international ethical guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals, including the ARRIVE guidelines, the European Union Directive 2010/63/EU, and the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (NIH Publications No 8023, revised 1978). The study also complied with the Mexican Official Standard NOM-062-ZOO-1999 for the use and care of laboratory animals. All animals used in this study were obtained from the animal facility of the Escuela Nacional de Ciencias Biológicas (ENCB), Instituto Politécnico Nacional, México. They were housed under standard laboratory conditions and handled according to institutional and international guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals. All procedures were non-invasive, involving only behavioral testing without the administration of drugs or surgical interventions.
